ca.17.impact: The widening gap between Mary's Messianic expectations and Jesus' actual spiritual direction is a source of quiet, persistent family tension. As the years pass, Mary is increasingly hurt by her son's gradual rejection of her guidance regarding his life career. Jesus inclines more and more toward his (now deceased) father's view of a spiritual mission, which causes Mary pain she will carry for decades. His silent grief over this is deep.
ca.18.title: Social Maturity — Broader Community Influence
ca.18.event: Jesus demonstrates growing social wisdom and tact, becoming increasingly skillful with his siblings and neighbors. He continues all family financial responsibilities while teaching the younger children at home. He has longer, deeper periods of solitary prayer and meditation on the hillside. His preference for the company of older, thoughtful individuals deepens — he enjoys discussions on culture, economics, politics, and religion with mature adults who are always willing to engage him at length. He maintains active contact with caravan travelers, absorbing knowledge of distant lands and peoples.
ca.18.impact: Jesus' capacity to relate meaningfully to people of all ages, classes, and cultural backgrounds is described as developing rapidly in these years. He is loved not only for fairness but for 'a rare and understanding sympathy that betokened love and bordered on discreet compassion.' He continues to be the recognized moral leader among his peers. His music — especially harp playing — remains a beloved community gift.
ca.19.title: Second Jerusalem Passover — Temple Scholars Again
ca.19.event: Jesus attends the Passover in Jerusalem for the second time, now as the responsible adult accompanying Mary (Joseph having died). He again engages teachers in the Temple with searching theological questions. July: John the Baptist, now 18, comes to Jerusalem to study; Jesus and John meet briefly and discuss the coming kingdom. Jesus makes a deep impression on the Jewish scholars he encounters but remains firmly committed to returning to his family responsibilities in Nazareth. He is becoming widely recognized in Jerusalem circles as an unusually thoughtful young man from Galilee.
ca.19.impact: At each Jerusalem visit, Jesus' impact on Temple scholars deepens. His questions consistently probe the spiritual meaning behind ritual observance — anticipating the transformative character of his later ministry. He is regularly invited to read the Scriptures at Sabbath services in the Nazareth synagogue, being master of all three languages: Aramaic, Greek, and Hebrew.
ca.20.title: Family Approaching Independence — Intensive Scriptural Study
ca.20.event: James, now 15, is increasingly capable of assisting with the carpenter shop. Jesus begins to perceive a gradual path toward eventual release from total family dependence. He attends the Passover in Jerusalem and engages rabbinical scholars. He conducts an intensive private study of the Hebrew Scriptures, the Septuagint, and other religious literature available in Nazareth. He prays regularly on the hillside northwest of town, deepening his communion with the Universal Father. Outwardly he appears a conventional carpenter and respected community member; inwardly his spiritual world is rich, complex, and increasingly clear.
ca.20.impact: Jesus is carefully calibrating the timing of his eventual public ministry, ensuring his family will be genuinely self-sufficient before he departs. He resolves all theological and philosophical questions independently, relying entirely on his own spiritual insight and communion with the Father — he has no human teacher. He possesses 'an unerring ability for the recognition of truth' and never hesitates to embrace truth regardless of its source.
ca.21.title: James Takes Responsibility — Transition Planning Begins
ca.21.event: James, now 16 and capable, begins assuming increasing responsibility for the carpenter shop and the care of the younger siblings. Jesus begins planning more concretely for the time when he can leave family duties and begin his public mission. He continues his wide reading and intensive prayer life. He attends the Passover in Jerusalem, deepening his understanding of Jewish religious life and its profound spiritual needs. He is now fully grown — a mature, physically impressive, and intellectually formidable young man of twenty years.
ca.21.impact: The transition of family leadership to James is gradual and deliberate — Jesus refuses to act hastily, ensuring each sibling is adequately settled before increasing his own freedom. He never wholly neglects the recreational and social aspects of life even while preparing for his mission. His humor, warmth, and storytelling gift make him a treasured presence in the community. Neighbors seek his counsel on personal and family matters.
ca.22.title: Expanded Caravan Work — Growing Freedom from Family
ca.22.event: Jesus increasingly takes caravan work — traveling with commercial caravans as a translator, guide, and general assistant. His fluency in Aramaic, Greek, and Hebrew makes him extremely valuable on regional trade routes. He meets people from across the Roman Empire and beyond. These journeys deepen his understanding of the diverse peoples, cultures, and religious traditions of the known world. He continues to send financial support back to his family in Nazareth and returns home periodically.
ca.22.impact: The caravan years represent a pivotal broadening of Jesus' human experience. He engages with merchants, soldiers, philosophers, and sincere truth-seekers from many lands — directly preparing him for a universal ministry. He develops the ability to communicate profound spiritual truths in terms immediately accessible to people of vastly different cultural and educational backgrounds. This gift will define his public teaching ministry.
ca.23.title: Works at Zebedee's Boatyard — Capernaum
ca.23.event: Jesus works for a period at the boatyard of Zebedee in Capernaum, applying his carpentry skills to the construction of fishing boats. He becomes well acquainted with the Zebedee family — whose sons James and John will later become two of his closest apostles. He lives near the Sea of Galilee and gains intimate knowledge of the fishing industry and the culture of Galilean lakeside communities. He continues his intense study and prayer life, his spiritual vision deepening steadily.
ca.23.impact: The Zebedee household becomes a key relationship that will later serve as a primary base for his Galilean ministry. His time building boats by the Sea of Galilee gives him practical knowledge of fishermen's daily lives and builds personal connections that will prove crucial in the calling of his apostles. Zebedee himself comes to deeply respect and admire Jesus during this period.
ca.24.title: Mediterranean Journey — Departs with Gonod & Ganid
ca.24.event: Jesus meets Gonod, a wealthy merchant from India, and his son Ganid. Gonod engages Jesus as a personal interpreter and tutor for his son for a long journey. The route: Jerusalem → Caesarea (by sea) → Alexandria → across the Mediterranean → Rome. In Alexandria Jesus visits the great library, meets teachers of Hellenistic philosophy and theology, and engages deeply with the intellectual life of that city. He composes personal essays on religious topics during the sea voyages. He studies Stoicism, Epicureanism, Cynicism, Neoplatonism, and Egyptian mystery religions firsthand.
ca.24.impact: The journey with Gonod and Ganid is the most intellectually expansive chapter of Jesus' life. He discusses religion, philosophy, and the nature of God with people of every background encountered along the way. He never reveals his identity or divine mission but consistently points all inquirers to the universal Father. His method of personal spiritual ministry — meeting each individual precisely at their own spiritual level — is refined and perfected during this extended journey.
ca.25.title: In Rome — One-on-One Ministry Across All Society
ca.25.event: Jesus spends significant time in Rome, the heart of the Empire. He mingles with all classes of Roman society — slaves, soldiers, philosophers, merchants, and officials. He visits synagogues, pagan temples, and philosophical schools. He has notable personal conversations with numerous individuals, consistently pointing each one to the reality of the loving Universal Father. He observes Roman law, governance, culture, and the diverse religious movements flourishing in the capital. His companion Ganid records many of his religious conversations and teachings in writing.
ca.25.impact: Jesus' time in Rome represents his most extensive engagement with Gentile civilization. He is deeply moved by the spiritual hunger of Rome's population and the inadequacy of both official Roman religion and the mystery cults to satisfy it. He gives no public teaching and claims no special identity, but his personal one-on-one ministry quietly touches many lives. He comes to see Rome as an eventual field for the proclamation of his gospel — and history will prove him right.
ca.26.title: Return from Mediterranean — Farewell to Gonod and Ganid
ca.26.event: The Mediterranean journey concludes. Jesus parts warmly from Gonod and Ganid, who return to India carrying with them seeds of spiritual truth that will eventually bear fruit. Jesus makes his way back to Palestine and visits his family in Nazareth, now well established under James' management. He checks on each sibling and ensures the family is thriving. He begins to feel with increasing clarity the pull of his public mission and knows its inauguration is now approaching.
ca.26.impact: Ganid has been deeply and permanently influenced by Jesus' teaching and carries those seeds back to India. Jesus has now encountered firsthand virtually every major civilization, religion, and philosophical tradition of the Mediterranean world. He has developed the capacity to speak to every kind of person with wisdom, warmth, and penetrating insight. The final preparatory phase of his life now begins in earnest.
ca.27.title: Continued Travels — Deepening Spiritual Integration
ca.27.event: Jesus continues to travel and work, supplementing the family's income and completing his personal preparation. He visits various regions of Palestine and neighboring areas, gaining detailed, intimate knowledge of the land and its people. He spends increasing periods in solitary prayer and communion with the Universal Father. He begins developing more precisely the specific form and content of his forthcoming public proclamation of the kingdom of heaven — what it is, who it is for, and how it will be presented.
ca.27.impact: These later travel years represent Jesus' final integration of all his accumulated human experience into a coherent and compelling vision for his ministry. He is by now extraordinarily well prepared — humanly, intellectually, emotionally, and spiritually — for what is to come. The combination of breadth (wide travel, diverse encounter) and depth (intimate family responsibility for sixteen years) is unique in the preparation of any religious teacher in recorded history.
ca.28.title: Caspian Sea Journey — Eastern Religions Explored
ca.28.event: January: Jesus departs with a merchant for the Caspian Sea region on his final extended travel journey. He travels through Mesopotamia, Persia, and the Caspian coastlands. He engages deeply with Zoroastrianism, Mithraism, and other Eastern religious traditions, meeting directly with their adherents and priests. He returns later in the year, having confirmed his conviction that the concept of a loving Universal Father is accessible — and resonant — to all peoples regardless of their religious tradition or cultural background.
ca.28.impact: The Caspian journey completes Jesus' survey of the major world religions. He has now engaged firsthand with Judaism, Hellenistic philosophy, Egyptian religion, Roman religion, mystery cults, and Zoroastrianism. His emerging universal gospel transcends every one of these while honoring the genuine truth within each. This journey marks the easternmost extent of his travels and the completion of his experiential preparation.
ca.29.title: Leaves Nazareth Permanently — Returns to Zebedee's
ca.29.event: March: Jesus takes permanent leave of his family in Nazareth, entrusting the household to James' care. He returns to work at Zebedee's boatyard in Capernaum. August 17: John the Baptist, age 28, begins his wilderness preaching ministry at the Jordan. Jesus follows John's rapidly growing movement with keen interest. He works at the boatyard while continuing his intense spiritual preparation and prayer life. He avoids all public religious activity, preferring to complete his inner preparation quietly and without fanfare.
ca.29.impact: Jesus' departure from Nazareth is permanent — he will return only for brief visits. The transition from 'the carpenter of Nazareth' to 'the teacher of Galilee' is now visibly and irreversibly underway. His relationship with the Zebedee family deepens further, cementing the bonds of trust and affection that will support his early ministry. John's wilderness preaching creates a spiritual awakening across Palestine that prepares the ground for everything Jesus is about to do.
ca.30.title: At Zebedee's — Awaiting the Father's Appointed Time
ca.30.event: Jesus continues working at Zebedee's boatyard, living in the Capernaum area throughout this year. He is now 28 years old — approaching the moment of public ministry. He follows closely the growing ministry of John the Baptist in the wilderness of Judea and the Jordan valley. He maintains his daily prayer life and the inner work of spiritual preparation. He is described as working steadily and patiently, 'waiting for the Father's time' for the beginning of his public mission. December: He begins making his way toward John.
ca.30.impact: The period at Zebedee's is characterized by quiet waiting and watchful, purposeful preparation. Jesus is entirely clear about his mission and its imminent inauguration but will not move ahead of the Universal Father's timing by a single day. This patient waiting — while humanly difficult — is itself an expression of the perfect trust in the Father's plan that will characterize his entire public ministry. 'Not my will, but yours' is already his settled disposition.
ca.31.title: Final Farewell to Family — Lays Down His Tools Forever
ca.31.event: Early March: Jesus attends the wedding of a relative in Cana — the last family gathering he will attend as one of them. He says his final farewells to each family member. April 1: Jesus departs on a final caravan journey and arrives in Capernaum on April 1, A.D. 25. He lays down his carpentry tools at Zebedee's boatyard for the last time, publicly declaring he will not return to the trade. He has spent approximately sixteen years providing for his family — far longer than his public ministry will last. He prepares to seek out John the Baptist and begin his public mission without reservation.
ca.31.impact: Jesus' formal departure from all carpentry and trade work is definitive and irreversible. The family is now genuinely self-sufficient under James' leadership — all younger siblings are grown, settled, and provided for. Jesus is free at last to devote himself entirely to his Father's business. He has fulfilled every human obligation before embarking on his divine mission — a completeness of preparation that is itself a profound spiritual lesson.
ca.32.title: Mount Hermon — Triumph over All Temptation
ca.32.event: Mid-August: Jesus establishes his camp near Beit Jenn in the foothills of Mount Hermon and spends approximately six weeks in solitary preparation and spiritual communion. He confronts and achieves complete victory over three supreme, archetypal temptations: (1) The Material Temptation — using divine power for personal benefit or to win followers through bread and spectacle; (2) The Intellectual Temptation — performing miracles to compel belief rather than invite faith; (3) The Spiritual Temptation — compromising truth for political power and worldly dominion. He achieves final, absolute victory over all three. Celestial beings attend him upon his descent.
ca.32.impact: The Hermon experience is the culminating event of Jesus' entire pre-ministry preparation — the final moral qualification for universal sovereignty. The Urantia Book records this as one of the most significant events in the entire history of Nebadon. Lucifer and Satan are forced to acknowledge defeat. The universe observes in awe. Note: this is the REAL temptation event — the forty days after baptism (commonly described in the Gospels) are devoted to finalizing ministry plans, NOT to temptation battles.
ca.33.title: Baptism by John — Public Ministry Officially Begins
ca.33.event: January 12: Jesus visits John's camp; the two spend the night discussing the kingdom of heaven. January 14 (Monday), noon: John baptizes Jesus in the Jordan River. At the moment of baptism, a voice from heaven declares 'This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased,' and the Spirit descends in the form of a dove. John recognizes Jesus as the one for whom he has been preparing the way. Jesus then enters forty days of withdrawal — not battling temptation, but receiving his bestowal commission from Gabriel and finalizing his detailed plans for the public ministry ahead.
ca.33.impact: The baptism marks the formal inauguration of Jesus' public work and the public proclamation of his divine sonship. The Urantia Book identifies A.D. 26 as the fifteenth year of Tiberius' actual reign — precisely consistent with Luke 3:1. The forty-day withdrawal is devoted entirely to settling the final details of his ministry plan. He emerges with a clear, comprehensive program for the proclamation of the kingdom of the heavenly Father.
ca.34.title: First Disciples — Wedding at Cana — Temple Cleansing
ca.34.event: February 23: Jesus begins gathering his first disciples. Andrew and Simon (Peter) are among the first called. He attends a wedding in Cana of Galilee where, at Mary's request, he transforms water into wine — his first public miracle, which strengthens the disciples' faith. He and his disciples travel to Capernaum, then to Jerusalem for the Passover, where he drives out the money changers and animal sellers from the Temple courts. June: He formally calls six apostles and sends them out two by two for the first evangelistic missions. June 23: He gives the first group their final instructions. Capernaum is established as his primary base of Galilean operations.
ca.34.impact: The wedding at Cana establishes the characteristic pattern of Jesus' miracles — performed in response to genuine human need, never for display or to compel belief. The Temple cleansing serves notice that his mission will directly challenge entrenched religious institutionalism. His deliberate choice of Galilean fishermen and common workers as apostles reflects his consistent preference for those uncontaminated by the rigidity of rabbinical formalism.
ca.35.title: Ordination of the Twelve — Sermon on the Mount
ca.35.event: January 12: Jesus formally ordains all twelve apostles in a full-day ceremony on a hillside near Capernaum. He delivers the Ordination Sermon — the Sermon on the Mount — centered on the eight Beatitudes, which constitute the most radical moral charter in human religious history. January 19: The first systematic Galilean preaching tour begins. Jesus heals many as he travels — lepers, paralytics, those with fever. He teaches consistently in synagogues and open countryside. The entire year of A.D. 27 is devoted to establishing the foundations of the kingdom movement across Galilee.
ca.35.impact: The Beatitudes represent the most radical reorientation of human values ever proclaimed — shifting the axis of religion from external law-keeping to internal transformation, from tribal privilege to universal brotherhood. The pace of ministry is relentless: Jesus simultaneously teaches, heals, trains apostles, and manages rapidly growing opposition from religious authorities, all while maintaining his own daily life of prayer and communion with the Father.
ca.36.title: Galilean Peak — Parables, Miracles & Rising Opposition
ca.36.event: The height of Jesus' Galilean popularity. He teaches the great kingdom parables — the Sower, the Mustard Seed, the Leaven, the Hidden Treasure, the Pearl of Great Price. He calms a violent storm on the Sea of Galilee. He raises the widow's son at Nain. He heals the Gadarene demoniac. He heals a paralytic lowered through the roof, declaring his authority to forgive sins — provoking the Pharisees' first formal charge of blasphemy. November 2: The Gilboa camp is broken up. The Sanhedrin in Jerusalem organizes its opposition into a coordinated, sustained campaign.
ca.36.impact: Jesus' miracles serve multiple, layered purposes simultaneously: revealing the Father's compassionate nature, demonstrating the reality and power of the kingdom, and responding to genuine human suffering. He consistently and firmly refuses to perform miracles 'on demand' as proof of identity. His parables are artfully designed to communicate spiritual truth to those ready to receive it while leaving others to ponder in their own time.
ca.37.title: John Beheaded — Feeding 5,000 — Peter's Confession
ca.37.event: January 10: John the Baptist is executed by Herod Antipas. Jesus grieves deeply and temporarily withdraws with his apostles. He feeds over 5,000 people with five barley loaves and two fish; the crowd attempts to make him king by force. He firmly refuses. He walks on water to his disciples caught in a storm. He delivers the 'Bread of Life' discourse in Capernaum, after which many followers withdraw. Late summer, near Caesarea Philippi: Peter confesses 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.' Jesus declares he will build his church upon this faith and begins teaching plainly about his coming suffering and death.
ca.37.impact: The feeding of the 5,000 and Peter's confession together mark the decisive turning point of the ministry: public popularity peaks and then splits sharply. Jesus' refusal of political kingship permanently disappoints those expecting a military Messiah. Peter's confession represents the apostolic community's arrival at genuine, articulate faith in Jesus' divine identity — a milestone toward which Jesus has been patiently leading them throughout the preceding two years of ministry.
ca.38.title: Transfiguration — Final Jerusalem Ministry — Raising of Lazarus
ca.38.event: Early: The Transfiguration on Mount Hermon — Peter, James, and John witness Jesus' divine radiance; Moses and Elijah appear; the Father's voice is heard again. May 22: Jesus departs for Jerusalem for the final time. He cleanses the Temple a second time. He teaches daily in the Temple courts with extraordinary authority. He raises Lazarus of Bethany from death — his most dramatic and public miracle — which precipitates the Sanhedrin's formal, final decision to arrest and execute him. He teaches on the Good Shepherd, the Mount of Olives discourse, and the kingdom's nature. He commends the widow's two-coin offering as the greatest act of generosity he has witnessed.
ca.38.impact: The raising of Lazarus is Jesus' most complete public demonstration of divine power — and it seals his earthly fate. The Sanhedrin formally resolves: 'It is expedient that one man should die for the people.' The Transfiguration — on the same Mount Hermon where Jesus overcame temptation — strengthens the three apostles for the ordeal ahead and provides cosmic confirmation of Jesus' identity to the observing universe. Jesus enters this final phase with full foreknowledge and perfect composure.
ca.39.title: Triumphal Entry into Jerusalem — Final Week Teachings
ca.39.event: Sunday, April 2: Jesus enters Jerusalem riding on a donkey, acclaimed by crowds with palm branches — 'Hosanna to the Son of David!' He weeps openly over Jerusalem, foreseeing its future destruction. He teaches daily in the Temple precincts throughout Passover week. Religious authorities attempt to trap him with questions about Roman taxes, resurrection, the greatest commandment, and his own authority. He warns publicly against the hypocrisy of scribes and Pharisees. He identifies himself to the crowds in unmistakably divine terms.
ca.39.impact: The triumphal entry deliberately fulfills Zechariah 9:9 — on a humble donkey rather than a war horse — an unmistakable proclamation that his kingship is of an entirely different order from anything the crowd expects. His public weeping over Jerusalem reveals both the depth of his love for his people and his clear foreknowledge of the suffering that their rejection of the kingdom will bring upon the city within a generation.
ca.40.title: The Last Supper — Gethsemane — Arrest
ca.40.event: Thursday evening, April 6: Jesus shares the Last Supper with the twelve in an upper room. He washes the disciples' feet as the supreme model of servant leadership. He institutes the Lord's Supper with bread and wine, establishing the new covenant. He delivers the Farewell Discourse: 'I am the way, the truth, and the life.' He prays the High Priestly Prayer for his disciples and all future believers. In Gethsemane he prays in great anguish: 'Not my will, but yours be done.' Judas arrives with soldiers; Jesus is arrested. All the apostles flee.
ca.40.impact: The Gethsemane prayer represents the supreme expression of Jesus' human nature — genuine anguish at the prospect of suffering and death — perfectly resolved in trust and submission to the Father's will. The Last Supper becomes the paradigmatic act of Christian worship for all subsequent generations. The betrayal by Judas Iscariot for thirty pieces of silver fulfills Jesus' own earlier warning that one of the twelve would deliver him up. Peter's three denials fulfil Jesus' prediction exactly.
ca.41.title: Trial — Crucifixion — 'It Is Finished'
ca.41.event: Before dawn: Illegal night trial before Annas, then Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin. Morning: Pilate questions Jesus, finds no legal fault, but yields to mob pressure. Jesus is scourged, mocked, and crowned with thorns. 9:00 AM: Crucifixion begins at Golgotha. Simon of Cyrene carries the cross. Two criminals are crucified alongside him. The inscription: 'Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.' Noon–3 PM: Darkness covers the land. ~3:00 PM: Jesus cries 'It is finished — Father, into your hands I commit my spirit' and breathes his last. The Temple veil tears from top to bottom. An earthquake occurs. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him in a new tomb before sunset.
ca.41.impact: The Urantia Book identifies the crucifixion as the single most significant event in all of human history — the supreme revelation of the Father's unconditional love. Jesus' forgiveness of his executors ('Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do') and his promise to the repentant criminal ('Today you will be with me in Paradise') exemplify the entire gospel in its most concentrated, crystalline form. His death coincides with the hour of the Passover lamb sacrifice in the Temple.
ca.42.title: Resurrection — The Empty Tomb — 'He Is Risen'
ca.42.event: Sunday, April 9, at 2:02 AM: The morontia form of Jesus rises from Joseph's sealed, guarded tomb. At dawn, Mary Magdalene arrives to find the stone rolled away. Angels announce: 'He is not here — he is risen.' Mary Magdalene receives the first personal appearance. Peter and John run to verify the empty tomb. Jesus appears to two disciples on the road to Emmaus. Evening: Jesus appears to all apostles except Thomas in the locked upper room — 'Peace be unto you.' Over forty days he makes nineteen distinct post-resurrection appearances to individuals and groups across Palestine and Galilee.
ca.42.impact: The Urantia Book distinguishes the resurrection as a true transformation: Jesus' physical body is reorganized and transmuted into morontia form, escaping the sealed tomb. This is fundamentally different from a mere resuscitation of a corpse. Simultaneously, the first complete dispensational resurrection roll call of Urantia's sleeping survivors takes place — the most sweeping planetary spiritual event since the times of Adam and Eve. The resurrection is the definitive, irrefutable proof of the reality of the kingdom and the eternal survival of the human soul.
ca.43.title: Ascension — Pentecost — Birth of the Church
ca.43.event: April 9 – May 18 (forty days): Jesus makes nineteen recorded post-resurrection appearances. He teaches about the kingdom, commissions the apostles ('Go and make disciples of all nations'), and explains the Scriptures in light of all that has occurred. May 18: The Ascension from the Mount of Olives. Jesus is received into a cloud and disappears. Angels announce: 'This same Jesus will come again in like manner.' May 28 (Pentecost): The Spirit of Truth is poured out upon the disciples in the upper room. Tongues of fire appear. Peter preaches; approximately 3,000 believe and are baptized. The Christian community is born in a single day.
ca.43.impact: The Ascension marks the end of Jesus' morontia career on Urantia and his return to Nebadon as its supreme and unconditional Sovereign — confirmed by Paradise. The outpouring of the Spirit of Truth at Pentecost fulfills his promise in John 16:7 and constitutes the birth of the church as a spirit-indwelt, universal community. The transition is complete: from a personal teacher-disciple relationship to a universal, cosmic spiritual presence alive within every sincere human heart.
